new_statements.rule_in_words: Yalálag Zapotec is a tone language (High, Low, Falling). Avelino gives no explicit stress-placement rule; his statements presuppose one stressed (primary-stress) syllable per content word, which is the root/stem syllable: roots are typically monosyllabic, the stressed nucleus is bimoraic (long vowel, diphthong, or vowel plus coda), and only the primary-stressed syllable can carry Falling tone. Bisyllabic Spanish loans are transcribed with stress on the syllable that was stressed in Spanish (e.g. ka'ba3, ku'pad, pan'dank, sep'tjembr, p. 154), which ends up as the word-final/stem syllable. Provisionally: stress is morphologically fixed on the (usually monosyllabic) root/stem syllable, not on affixes or clitics; a positional label cannot be assigned from this source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only one remark: the infinitive prefix w- before vowel-initial stems is 'a very short gesture, without independent (secondary) stress' and is not parsed as a separate syllable (p. 144).
new_statements.exceptions: Loan word par'jid < Spanish pálido is called 'still problematic' because Spanish stress is initial but the YZ form keeps the final syllable (p. 156). No native-word exceptions discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern content words/roots and stems (lexical word level) and loanword adaptation; no discussion of phrase-level accent. Tone, not stress, is the contrastive prosody; stress is treated as a prosodic condition on tone-bearing and syllable weight.
new_statements.identity_note: Avelino 2004 describes the Zapotec of Villa Hidalgo Yalálag itself (speakers recorded in Yalálag and in the Los Angeles diaspora), i.e. yala1267/zpu proper. Hernández Andrade 2011 describes two varieties spoken in San Juan Jaltepec (Choapan district), one of Yalálag origin and one of Santa María Yahuivé/Choapan origin (zpc); it contains no stress statement.
